en.title: Grant Morrison Calls for More Sci-Fi in Green Lantern Series
en.summary: Legendary comic writer Grant Morrison has voiced his critiques of HBO's Green Lantern series, lamenting a perceived lack of cosmic scope. He argues the show should lean into its science fiction roots rather than a grounded aesthetic.
en.body:
## Morrison's Cosmic Critique

**Grant Morrison**, a writer whose name is synonymous with groundbreaking runs on DC Comics' cosmic characters, has shared his thoughts on HBO's **Green Lantern** series. While acknowledging the show's critical success and its surprising deviation from typical superhero fare towards a more grounded, character-driven narrative, Morrison feels this approach misses the core potential of the Green Lantern mythos. He believes the series, which has been lauded for its gritty tone reminiscent of **True Detective**, is leaning too heavily on exposition and not enough on the visual spectacle that defines the emerald guardians of the universe.

Morrison, who previously engaged in a creative dialogue with showrunner Damon Lindelof regarding the series' direction, recently watched the first episode and shared his observations on his blog. His primary concern remains consistent: the show prioritizes "tell, not enough show." He specifically points to the absence of the iconic costumes and the vibrant, otherworldly ring effects that are fundamental to the Green Lantern experience. For Morrison, a Green Lantern story inherently demands a grand, cosmic scale that the current iteration seems hesitant to embrace.

> "Otherwise on this outing, way too much tell, not enough show, and those comparisons to True Detective, invoking season 1 of that, show, only worked against Lanterns. The lack of costumes and ring effects"

## What This Means for Lanterns Fans

Morrison's critique resonates with a segment of the fanbase who cherish the expansive, imaginative universe the Green Lanterns inhabit. While the grounded approach has garnered praise for its accessibility and compelling performances, it risks alienating readers who came to the property for its inherent science fiction grandeur. The Green Lantern Corps are intergalactic peacekeepers, tasked with policing the vastness of space, encountering alien species, and navigating complex cosmic phenomena. To reduce this potential to a more terrestrial mystery, as Morrison suggests the show has done, feels like a missed opportunity to showcase the unique visual and narrative possibilities that only a space opera can offer. The debate highlights a fundamental question for comic book adaptations: how much should they adhere to the source material's established tone and visual identity versus forging a new path for a different medium?

## Looking Ahead

With **Grant Morrison**'s vocal opinion now public, it will be interesting to see if the **Green Lantern** series addresses these criticisms in future episodes or seasons. Whether the show will embrace more of its cosmic heritage or continue on its current trajectory remains to be seen, but the conversation is undoubtedly sparking renewed interest in the character's rich, interstellar history. Details regarding future episodes and plot developments have not yet been announced.

The series that is often more True Detective than DCU has already caught quite a few people by surprise with its grounded tone, character-driven narrative, and exceptional performances. It’s slowly revealing its mythology, but if it wasn’t for the name on the box, you could almost hide the fact it’s a Green Lantern show. However, that approach hasn’t quite worked for everyone. Comics writer Grant Morrison (whose many notable works include a legendary run on the Green Lantern) has long been one of the show’s most notable critics, and previously got into a bit of a back-and-forth with Lanterns co-showrunner Damon Lindelof over the series’ creative direction. Well, Morrison has finally watched Lanterns ‘ first episode and recently shared his thoughts about it on his blog . While he came away from the series with a largely mixed opinion, his central criticism of the show remains largely unchanged. “Otherwise on this outing, way too much tell, not enough show, and those comparisons to True Detective , invoking season 1 of that, show, only worked against Lanterns ,” Morrison writes. “The lack of costumes and ring effects was glaring but easily explained by budgetary constraints and a desire to create some distance between this and the unsuccessful Ryan Reynolds Green Lantern film… which only begs the question of why try to make a Green Lantern show on a budget at all? DC has a ton of ‘ground level’ heroes, or characters with low level gimmick powers to choose from, so why take this low-fi route with a franchise that should be competing with Star Trek or Star Wars ?” Morrison’s criticisms are, of course, ultimately his opinion, though they do bring up a few interesting talking points. Namely, the recent emphasis on ground or street level heroics (something the Spider-Man: Brand New Day team also expressed an interest in emphasizing) and the general concern that we may not get a grander and more bombastic take on The Green Lantern while Lanterns remains a hit for DC. While asking why you would make a Green Lantern show on a budget at all is a hyperbolic question, it will be interesting to see if this is the definitive live-action tonal take we get of the character in the James Gunn era for the studio.
